Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Rajan has been a fisherman for forty years, his hands calloused from nets and his face weathered by the sun and sea off the Oregon coast. At fifty-eight, he’d always thought of himself as sturdy, as reliable as the tides. But the man who sits in the consulting room is a stranger to that version of himself. Six months ago, on a slick, rain-soaked road, that man was shattered. He was driving his truck back from the market, the day’s catch sold, when a sedan sped through a stop sign. Rajan remembers the brief, almost polite eye contact with the other driver, a young man who smiled a moment before impact. Then came the screech of metal, the explosive pop of the passenger-side window, and a sudden, terrible silence that was deeper and more absolute than any quiet he had ever known on the open water.

In the aftermath, the memories refused to settle into the past. They are not stories he can tell but ambushes that happen to him. When a car backfires down the street, he is no longer in his living room but back in the twisted cab of his truck, the coppery scent of blood in his nostrils, the weight of his own body pinned against the door. The terror is not a recollection; it is a fresh wave that drowns him, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. He knows what happened, can see the sequence of events, but when he tries to explain it to his daughter, the words jam in his throat. He is left gesturing, his hands sketching the shape of a car, his voice failing him. He feels the event is happening right now, a permanent present tense he cannot escape.

This sense of imminent catastrophe has bled into every corner of his life. His small house, once a sanctuary filled with memories of his late wife, now feels porous and unsafe. He finds himself on guard constantly, checking the locks, peering through the curtains at any passing car. He has come to believe that people are not what they seem; that friendly smile from the other driver was a mask for the violence that followed, and now he sees that same potential for betrayal in every stranger’s face. At the docks, a place that was once his second home, he now scans the crowd ceaselessly, his eyes darting from face to face, searching for a threat he cannot name. A simple "Good morning" from a tourist wanting to buy a fish directly from the boat sends a jolt of panic through him, and he turns away, mumbling an excuse.

His work, once his pride, has become a source of torment. Out on the water, the familiar hum of the diesel engine is a comfort, but if the engine stalls or the wind dies, the resulting quiet is no longer peaceful. It is the same charged silence that filled the air after the crash, a vacuum that he is certain will be filled by another cataclysm. He no longer trusts the vessel that has supported him for decades, and worse, he no longer trusts his own body to navigate it. A sudden ache in his shoulder is not arthritis but a sign of collapse; a skipped heartbeat is not from exertion but a prelude to failure. The man who could read the weather in the clouds now feels like a fragile instrument, easily broken. This isn't him. He feels he doesn't know himself anymore, a ghost haunting the life of a more capable man.

His world has shrunk. He stopped driving immediately. He avoids the news, especially stories of accidents or loss, the mention of which feels like a physical blow. His fishing buddies have learned not to talk about friends who have passed away in his presence after he abruptly walked out of a conversation, leaving a confused silence in his wake. This isolation is what finally brought him here. His daughter, seeing her once-vital father become a recluse, pleaded with him to seek help. Rajan came not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that the strong, steady fisherman is gone for good, replaced by this fearful, brittle man who can no longer find his way.
